name: X Couloir (Southwest Face) / Standard Route

pitch_detail.notes: From the SW buttress base, ascend snow slopes toward the first bergschrund.
Cross a snow bridge and climb directly up the face of a ~50-ft serac.
Two roped 60m pitches through narrow gullies with runnel crossings.
Knife-edge arete requiring careful tool and crampon placement.
Final ~20 ft of scrambling on loose rock past crumbling rime-ice features to the summit.

descent_text: Most parties reverse the ascent line, downclimbing and rappelling the same southwest gully/couloir system (the X Couloir) back down into the southwest basin below the face. This is a real rappelling descent, not a walk-off: the most detailed documented descent (a repeat/'2nd descent' trip report) describes 10 double-rope rappels — 4 off pickets placed by the descending party, 1 off a sling around a rock, and 5 off pre-existing slings left around rock horns lower in the gully. Bring a rope long enough to rappel on doubled strands plus spare cord/webbing for building or backing up anchors, since fixed tat should never be trusted blindly. Anchors are a mix of natural (slung rock horns and blocks) and improvised (snow pickets), not bolted — expect to build some yourself. The exact rappel count is conditions-dependent: earlier-season parties with more continuous snow have gotten down with as few as 3 rappels off deadman/picket anchors and simul-downclimbing between them, while later-season, rockier conditions push the count up toward the 10-rappel figure above; budget for the higher number and extra anchor material. The gully funnels rockfall and is exposed to spindrift/small slides after storms, so descend early and move efficiently through the narrower constrictions. Once off the couloir, re-rope for the bergschrund and any crevassed ground on the way down to the treeline camp, then reverse the approach - down past East Rankin Lake and around Pt. 4481 on the old decommissioned road - back to FR-38. Do not descend north toward Heliotrope Ridge. With a camp in the Rankin Creek basin, going that way puts you on the opposite side of the mountain with a glacier between you and your camp.
approach: The X Couloir is most directly approached from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38); the less direct alternative starts at Heliotrope Ridge and reaches the southwest face through the Thunder Glacier cirque. Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start hiking/bushwhacking the old decommissioned road around Pt. 4481 toward Rankin Creek — snow travel (often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch) leads past East Rankin Lake (~5,120 ft) and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, near the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. From camp, an alpine start gets the team into the southwest basin and across the bergschrund crux while it's still cold and firm, climbing roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40° snow and a steep serac step in the X Couloir to the 9,085 ft summit. Total approach is on the order of 7 miles and 3,350 ft of gain to the basin camp. Important — access note: FR-38 (Middle Fork Nooksack River Road), damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since 27 July 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on 25 September 2026, and a separate seasonal gate at Wallace Creek (~mile 10) closes the road December 1-June 15 for elk calving; confirm current road status with the Mount Baker Ranger District (Glacier Public Service Center) before a trip, since the drivable road-end — and therefore the length of the approach — varies year to year.
overview: Lincoln Peak's SW Face route, known as the 'X Couloir' (sometimes referenced as 'X Couloir – Emancipation Proclamation'), is the historic line up this seldom-climbed, seriously loose Black Buttes summit. First climbed by Fred Beckey, Wesley Grande, John Rupley, and Herb Staley on July 22, 1956, it was the only documented route to the summit until a 2015 first ascent opened a second line on the NW Face. Only about a dozen ascents are known; the peak is guarded by near-vertical walls on every side.
beta: The historic standard route on Lincoln Peak; the only other line is a rarely formed northwest-face ice route. Approach via Rankin Creek Basin from FS Road 38. Technical snow and ice climbing with significant avalanche risk. Route comprises multiple sections: 30-40 degree initial snowfields, crux serac obstacle requiring 70-85 degree ice climbing (50 feet high), hidden gully with 2-4 foot deep runnels, narrow exposed snow aretes with steep drop-offs, and final 50-degree gully to summit rocks. Climb early morning when snow is frozen; conditions deteriorate rapidly with afternoon warming.
gear: small rack of nuts and cams (4 small cams)
